summary: Elevates RFC 7344 to the Standards Track and adds a method for initial DNSSEC trust setup and for removing a secure entry point, so a parent zone can manage a child's DS records.

eli5.summary: A child zone leaves a note for its parent saying which key to trust, so the parent can update it.

questions: what are cds and cdnskey records
how to remove a ds record
subtitle: How a child zone can ask its parent to add, change or remove DS records, including turning DNSSEC on and off.

tldr.problem: DS records in a parent zone often can only be changed through a registry or registrar, so child zones and third-party DNS operators struggle to switch DNSSEC on or off.
tldr.mechanism: The child publishes CDS or CDNSKEY records as an in-band request to synchronize the parent's DS records. The RFC lists parent acceptance policies for the first DS and defines a delete signal using algorithm 0.
tldr.outcome: It promotes RFC 7344 to the Standards Track and adds initial trust setup and removal of a secure entry point. It has since been updated by RFC 9615.

today: RFC 8078 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7344 and has itself been updated by RFC 9615.

sections.title: Why CDS and CDNSKEY Need More
sections.content:
CDS (Child DS) and CDNSKEY (Child DNSKEY) records, defined in RFC 7344, signal changes in secure entry points. They are one way to maintain delegations when the DNS operator has no other way to tell the parent that changes are needed. This RFC elevates RFC 7344 from Informational to Standards Track.

RFC 7344 lacks two things needed for full automation. It does not define how to establish initial trust, leaving each parent to invent an acceptance policy, and it has no 'delete' signal for the child to ask that DNSSEC be removed.

In this document, 'CDS' means either CDS or CDNSKEY. The two differ only in how the information is represented and who calculates the DS digest. 'Parent' means any entity authorized to insert DS records into the parent zone for the child, such as a Registrar, Reseller or Registry.
sections.eli5: The old system let a child say 'I changed my key'. It had no way to say 'I am new, trust me' or 'please stop checking me', so this RFC adds both.

sections.title: Introducing and Removing DS Records
sections.content:
Automated insertion of DS records has been limited because every change must pass through a Registry of the child zone's parent. The RFC says this hindered large-scale DNSSEC deployment by DNS hosters, since the child zone owner often cannot update such records.

Removal matters too. When a domain moves between DNS operators, DNSSEC sometimes has to be turned off. The RFC lists scenarios such as moving to an operator that is not DNSSEC-capable, moving between operators that use disjoint sets of signing algorithms (so an algorithm rollover cannot be done), or a domain holder who no longer wants DNSSEC. The lack of a 'remove my DNSSEC' option is cited as a reason some operators cannot deploy DNSSEC.

Turning off DNSSEC reduces a domain's security, so it should be done carefully and the decision should be fully under the child's control.
sections.eli5: Moving to a new caretaker is hard if the old lock cannot be taken off. A way to say 'remove my lock' makes people more willing to use locks at all.

sections.title: The Three Uses of CDS
sections.content:
A domain wants its parent to do one of three things: enable DNSSEC validation by placing an initial DS RRset, roll over the KSK by updating the DS records (an ADD, a DELETE that keeps at least one DS RR, or a full REPLACE), or turn DNSSEC off by deleting all DS records.

Key rollover is covered by RFC 7344 and is considered the safest use, since it does not change the trust relationship. Introduction and removal are defined here, and because they create or end trust between parent and child they should be carefully implemented and monitored.

Publishing a CDS or CDNSKEY record signals that the child wants the corresponding DS records synchronized. Every parent should have an acceptance policy for the three cases. In short, the CDS RRset is an instruction to modify the DS RRset if the two differ. For rollover the policy is 'seeing' the record per RFC 7344; for delete it is seeing a validly signed CDS RRset with the delete operation.
sections.eli5: The child can ask for three things: 'start trusting me', 'I swapped my key', or 'stop trusting me'. The parent follows the note if it passes its checks.

sections.title: Parent Acceptance Policies for Enabling DNSSEC
sections.content:
The goal is to move the child from insecure to secure as soon as reasonably possible, so the time between the child publishing CDS/CDNSKEY and the parent publishing the DS should be as short as possible. How a third-party DNS operator authenticates and submits its information is outside the scope. The RFC then describes five example policies that assume notifications can be verified.

  • Authenticated channel: the parent is told via an authenticated UI or API that a CDS/CDNSKEY RRset exists, retrieves it and inserts the DS. Parents SHOULD NOT refuse updates that lack a matching DNSKEY yet, so a child can pre-publish a spare, possibly offline, key.
  • Extra checks: the parent checks the requester is allowed to ask, for example by comparing nameservers or sending email to the registrant. Extra checks should have proper rate limiting.
  • After delay: the parent monitors the CDS RRset over time, preferably from different vantage points, before accepting.
  • With challenge: the parent asks the requester to publish a record in the child zone to prove control, and checks it on all the child's nameservers from diverse locations.
  • From inception: for a brand-new delegation, the parent can publish the DS RRset together with the NS RRset so the child is never active in an insecure state.
sections.eli5: When someone new says 'trust me', the parent can ask the owner, wait and watch, ask for a secret handshake, or just accept at the very start. Each has a different level of care.

sections.title: The DNSSEC Delete Signal
sections.content:
The RFC defines the previously reserved DNS Security Algorithm Number 0, in the context of CDS and CDNSKEY, to mean that the entire DS RRset at the parent must be removed. The value stays reserved for DS and DNSKEY records. A validator that sees algorithm 0 in a DNSKEY or DS record must treat it as unknown, so the zone is treated as unsigned unless other algorithms are present.

A delete request MUST contain one RR with exactly these fields: CDS 0 0 0 0 or CDNSKEY 0 3 0 0. The keying material payload is a single 0, and the record is signed like any other CDS/CDNSKEY RRset. The 3 in the CDNSKEY record is the protocol value mandated by RFC 4034.

Once the parent has verified the RRset and it passes other acceptance tests, the parent MUST remove the DS RRset. The child should then wait a sufficient time, depending on the parental TTLs, before starting to turn off DNSSEC.
sections.eli5: The 'please remove my lock' note has a fixed form made of zeros. Only that exact note counts as a removal request.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Turning off DNSSEC reduces security and should be a last resort for avoiding validation errors caused by mismatched DS and DNSKEY records. Re-establishing trust in a delegation can be hard and takes time, so all other options should be considered before finishing a rollover via an unsigned state. The RFC prefers operators to collaborate on a move, ideally with a KSK plus ZSK rollover; the unsigned route leaves the domain temporarily vulnerable to DNS spoofing.

A parent SHOULD have reasonable assurance that the CDS/CDNSKEY RRset used to bootstrap security is visible from a geographically and topologically diverse view, and SHOULD ensure the zone validates correctly once the DS is published. It might also email its contact addresses so a child administrator can cancel the request. Because legal frameworks vary, especially for TLDs, the RFC cannot give a definitive list of acceptance criteria; parents should pick the most secure method their situation allows while keeping it fully automated for third-party hosters.
sections.eli5: Switching the lock off is risky, so do it only if nothing else works. Before switching one on, the parent should look from many places to be sure the note is real.

sections.title: IANA Registration and Standards Track Promotion
sections.content:
IANA assigned entry number 0 in the 'DNS Security Algorithm Numbers' registry with the description 'Delete DS' and mnemonic DELETE. Zone Signing and Transaction Security are both marked N, and the references are RFC 4034, RFC 4398 and RFC 8078.

The RFC also records that, because experience showed CDS and CDNSKEY to be useful for deploying DNSSEC, RFC 7344 is elevated to the Standards Track.
sections.eli5: The official list of algorithm numbers now says that number 0 means 'delete'.
